                               STAFF’S RESPONSE TO EXCEPTIONS
                            TO THE CERTIFICATION OF STIPULATION


           COMES NOW the Advocacy Division (“Staff”) of the New Mexico Public Regulation

Commission (“Commission” or “NMPRC”) and, pursuant to 1.2.2.20(B)(5)(b) NMAC,

1.2.2.37(C) NMAC, and the Commission’s Order Granting Leave to File Responses to Exceptions

and Order Requiring Response to Staff’s Motion for Oral Argument issued on November 5, 2026,

respectfully submits this Response to the Statements of Exceptions filed by Southwestern Public

Service Company (“SPS”), the New Mexico Large Customer Group (“NMLCG”), and Louisiana

Energy Services, LLC and Federal Executive Agencies (“LES/FEA”).

I. INTRODUCTION & EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

           On October 23, 2026, the Hearing Examiners issued their Certification of Stipulation

(“Certification” or “Cert.”) in this docket which correctly adopted Staff’s positions on five

modifications1: (1) rejecting the stipulated volumetric "Energy-at-Source" allocator and ordering

that all solar Production Tax Credit (“PTC”) benefits be allocated among customer classes using

the demand-based AED-4CP Prod allocator2; (2) rejecting the stipulated single coincident peak

(“1-CP”) system load factor and retaining the status quo 4-CP system load factor in the Average

 and Excess Demand (“AED-4CP”) class cost-of-service study (“CCOSS”)3; (3) eliminating the

Planning Reserve Margin (“PRM”) divisor from the 12-CP jurisdictional allocator formula for the

Cunningham Battery Energy Storage System (“BESS”), awarding New Mexico retail customers

the full, un-derated 24.0 MW accredited capacity (“ACAP”) benefit;4 and (4)–(5) disallowing the

unsupported Community Solar Portal O&M expense and a portion of SPS’s rate case expenses. 5

         The Exceptions filed by SPS, NMLCG, and LES/FEA would undo these modifications.

They would let transmission-voltage classes capture 95.0% of solar PTC benefits while the

Residential class pays 18.55% of the facilities’ capital costs, shift approximately $2.3 million in

revenue requirement onto the Residential class, and restore unsupported expenses. The

modifications are supported by substantial evidence and correctly apply New Mexico law. Staff

requests that the Commission deny the Exceptions, affirm Finding Paragraph 9, and grant Staff’s

Exceptions and Motion for Oral Argument.

II. EXCEPTIONS TO SOLAR PRODUCTION TAX CREDIT (PTC) ALLOCATION
    A. Demanding Reinstatement of Energy-at-Source Allocator6

         In his initial, pre-filed Direct Testimony, SPS witness Taylor J. Hurt testified that

Production Tax Credits generated by solar facilities must be allocated among customer classes

using the demand-based AED-4CP Prod allocator.7 Hurt testified that because SPS proposed to

assign the base capital costs of the solar facilities (Cunningham and Plant X Solar) using the AED-

4CP Prod allocator, it is appropriate to match that allocator for the assignment of PTCs so that the

customer classes paying the base capital costs of the solar units receive their fair share of the PTC

 benefits in relation to the costs they pay.8 Hurt further testified that the AED-4CP Prod true-up

would occur in April of each year and be reflected in June fuel factors.9

         However, Section 1.11 Stipulation, abandons Witness Hurt’s pre-filed position and agreed

to allocate solar PTCs using a volumetric "Energy-at-Source" per-kWh allocator.10 Certification

page 61 states: “Stipulation Section 1.11 stipulates that “PTCs will be allocated on an energy

basis.” This means that PTCs will be allocated using the “Energy-at-Source” allocator, and this

allocator allocates the value of the PTCs according to the quantity of kWh used by a Voltage class.”

Under this stipulated volumetric approach, high-volume industrial classes, including NMLCG and

FEA/LES, will receive 95.0% of the solar PTC tax credits, while the Residential class receives

only 5.0% of the credits, despite being assigned 18.55% of the solar facilities' fixed capital

construction costs under the AED-4CP Prod demand allocator11 The Certification agreed with and

adopted Staff's position ruling that solar PTCs must be allocated using the AED-4CP Prod allocator

to ensure cost-benefit symmetry between capital cost responsibility and tax credit recovery.12

B. The Certification’s correctly applies cost causation
         Solar capital costs are classified as production demand costs and allocated by the AED-

4CP Prod allocator, under which the Residential class pays 18.55% of the capital revenue

requirement. The associated tax credits should follow the same allocator, so the Residential class

should receive 18.55% of the benefits. SPS and the Intervenors may argue that PTCs are earned

per MWh generated and therefore follow energy, but the PTCs offset the cost of the same capital

investment, and the benefit should follow the classes that pay for it (Cert. ¶ 184).

            The exceptions filed by SPS, NMLCG, and LES/FEA demanding the volumetric ”Energy-

at-Source” PTC allocator was correctly rejected by the Certification. Capital-intensive solar

facilities are constructed to satisfy system peak capacity demands and are classified as production

demand costs. In the class cost-of-service study, these fixed capital investments are allocated

among customer classes using the demand-based AED-4CP Prod allocator, resulting in the

Residential class paying 18.55% of the fixed capital revenue requirement. Allocating the

associated tax credits benefits should be the same. In other words, the residential class should

receive 18.55% of the benefits.

           The Stipulation, however, would allocate the benefits of the PTCs on a volumetric per-

kWh basis, which would unfairly allow high-volume transmission customers, such as NMLG and

FEA/LES to capture 95.0% of the tax benefits while contributing comparatively little to the peak-

demand capital costs that made the facilities possible. As SPS's own cost witness Hurt originally

admitted, matching the tax credit allocator to the capital cost allocator (AED-4CP Prod) is legally

necessary to ensure that customer classes paying for the solar facilities receive their fair share of

the tax benefits.13 Therefore, the Cert. ¶¶ 184 made the correct finding:

           This methodology ensures that the allocation of PTCs takes into account the relative
           monetary contributions from each rate class and uses the same allocator to assign
           both costs and benefits. And, similar to the recommendation on the use of the AED
           4-CP load factor, as opposed to the 1-CP load factor, this recommendation leans in
           the direction of protecting non large load customers from costs, and is a reasonable
           policy decision when the Commission is faced with a decision that has been argued
           from both sides by SPS.
III. RESPONSE TO EXCEPTIONS REGARDING COSS LOAD FACTOR AED 4-CP14

          In Section 1.11 of the Stipulation, the Signatories agreed to modify the AED cost-allocation

methodology by calculating the system load factor using a single coincident peak (1-CP) rather

than the historical four coincident peaks15 (4-CP). Staff witness Zigich opposed this because the

agreement in the Commission-approved stipulation in Case No. 25-00085-UT (Section I.1.3,

Condition C), SPS legally committed to convene a collaborative stakeholder working group with

Staff and Intervenors to evaluate and analyze alternatives to SPS's retail customer class cost

allocation, using the existing 4-CP allocator as the baseline. 16 Zigich maintained that if the

Stipulation § 1.11 is approved it would negate the agreement from the Stipulation in Case No. 25-

00085-UT. The agreed-upon stakeholder working group has not yet concluded its technical

evaluations or submitted recommendations to the Commission.17

         During cross-examination, SPS witness Alexander G. Trowbridge confirmed that shifting

from 4-CP to 1-CP produces a major cost reduction for only two customer classes: Primary General

and 115 kV Large General Service-Transmission (LGS-T), while shifting approximately

$2,300,000 in revenue requirement onto the Residential class. 18 While in his pre-filed Direct

Testimony, Staff witness Dr. Larry Blank recommended, only for future rate cases, the average

and excess demand allocation method could be calculated using the single system peak demand. .
19
     Under cross-examination, Dr. Blank clarified that he did not propose altering class cost

allocations in the current proceeding.20 The Certification adopted Staff’s position21 rejecting the

1-CP system load factor shift and retaining the status quo 4-CP system load factor pending

Finding 9(e)(i) are based upon a misstatement of Dr. Blank’s position.23

     A. The Certification’s rejection of the Stipulation Section 1.11 is based upon
        established law

        Under New Mexico administrative law and contract principles, a Commission-approved

stipulation constitutes a binding regulatory compact that cannot be unilaterally bypassed or

modified in a subsequent rate docket. .In Case No. 25-00085-UT, SPS and the intervenors agreed

to a formal stakeholder process to investigate class allocation alternatives prior to implementing

methodology shifts. The Signatories’ attempt to implement a 1-CP system load factor in Section

1.11 of the Stipulation constitutes an impermissible collateral attack on the Final Order in Case

No. 25-00085-UT.

        Furthermore, implementing the 1-CP shift in this docket violates NMSA 1978, Section 62-

8-6 by engineering an unjustified $2,300,000 cost shift onto captive residential ratepayers to

benefit high-load-factor industrial users. As stated above, contrary to the Intervenors’ claim that

Dr. Blank recommended 1-CP for this proceeding Dr. Blank explicitly limited his opinion to

“future rate cases” and affirmed that Staff’s direct case supported continuing the existing 4-CP

cost-of-service parameters. 24 SPS, NMLCG and LES/FEA did not meet their burden under

1.2.2.20(B)(4) NMAC to prove that the Stipulation’s agreement to cut out the 25-00085-UT

Stipulation’s working group process on this important issue is just and reasonable and in the public

interest. Therefore, the Hearing Examiners correctly enforced the 25-00085-UT prior Commission

order in Finding 9(e)(i) by retaining the 4-CP method until the working group and its report.

 IV. RESPONSE TO EXCEPTIONS REGARDING CERTIFICATION’S
MODIFICATION OF THE STIPULATION’S METHODOLOGY FOR CALCULATING
CUNNINGHAM BESS CAPACITY OFFSET25
A. SPS objects to the Certification's modification to calculate the capacity benefit from the
Cunningham BESS.
        Following the Public Utility Commission of Texas's rejection of the facility in Docket No.

55255, SPS, through its Application in this case, requested authority to directly assign 100% of

the capital and operating costs of the 36 MW/144 MWh Cunningham BESS to New Mexico retail

customers. 26 Staff’s direct case 27 conditionally supported 100% New Mexico cost assignment

provided New Mexico retail customers receive 100% of the accredited capacity (ACAP) benefits

(24.0 MW) as a direct credit against New Mexico's share of system production peak demand.

        Sections 1.3 and 1.17 of the Stipulation established a method for calculating the

Cunningham BESS jurisdictional 12-CP capacity credit that reduced the credit by dividing the

24.0 MW ACAP by (1 + seasonal PRM) (where seasonal PRM was set at 16% summer / 36%

winter), which diluted the capacity offset to 22.4 MW in summer and 21.0 MW in winter.28 SPS

filed Exception No. 3 asserting that failing to divide ACAP by (1 + PRM) creates an unearned

windfall for New Mexico retail customers. 29 Staff’s Opposition to the Stipulation opposed the

calculation on the basis that dividing the ACAP by 1+ PRM unfairly reduced the capacity credit

for New Mexico customers. The Hearing Examiners agreed and adopted Staff’s position in Finding

9(b)(i), determining that Southwest Power Pool (SPP) Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC)

accreditation already derates nameplate storage capacity down to 24.0 MW. For this reason, the

B. Certification upholds principles of cost causation and fairness to New Mexico customers
       There is no windfall. New Mexico customers pay 100% of the Cunningham BESS’s capital

costs, O&M expenses, and carrying charges in base rates, so cost causation entitles them to its full

capacity value. SPP accreditation already derates the 36 MW nameplate to 24.0 MW ACAP; a (1

+ PRM) divisor derates it a second time and denies New Mexico customers 1.6 MW (summer) to

3.0 MW (winter) of capacity credit for a resource they alone fund. That result is inconsistent with

NMSA 1978, Section 62-8-6 and the Commission’s Final Order in Case No. 25-00066-UT.31

V. SPS’S EXCEPTIONS REGARDING RATE CASE EXPENSES AND COMMUNITY
SOLAR PORTAL O&M32

A. SPS’s opposes disallowance of $265,322 Community Solar Portal O&M33
         In its Application, SPS requested $4,342,331 in rate case expenses amortized over two

years, which included a $200,000 generic category labeled “Other Company Expenses”34. The

Hearing Examiners in Finding 9(d)(i)–(ii): (1) disallowed the $200,000 “Other Company

Expenses” category as unverified; (2) applied a 26% disallowance to remaining expenses based

on historical variance analysis showing SPS consistently incurs only 74% of requested rate case

estimates; and (3) extended the amortization period from two to three years.

         In addition, SPS included $265,322 in annual Future Test Year (FTY) operating expenses

for a Community Solar Portal which Staff witness Peterson Brossy testified was hard-keyed into

a spreadsheet workpaper without any supporting calculations or written witness testimony

B. The Hearing Examiners correctly applied 17.1.3.14 NMAC in Finding 9(a)(i) by
disallowing the $265,322 Community Solar Portal expense.

        Pursuant to 17.1.3.14 NMAC, all Future Test Year filing data “shall be accompanied by

testimony and exhibits explaining and justifying quantities, assumptions, expectations, activity

changes, etc., and verifying the amounts used to support the future test year period are the utility's

most recently available data.” Under 17.1.3.17(A) & (C) NMAC, all FTY estimates must be fully

explained and supported by "verifiable evidence." SPS admitted on the record that no witness filed

explanatory testimony supporting this line item. Under New Mexico law, spreadsheet entries

lacking sponsoring witness testimony are legally unverified and do not comply with 17.1.3.14 and

do not fulfill the burden of proof required by NMSA 1978, Section 62-8-7(A). With respect to rate

case expenses, the Hearing Examiners acted well within their administrative discretion under

NMSA 1978, Section 62-8-1 by applying a 26% disallowance and a 3-year amortization period.

As noted by Staff evidence across SPS’s prior two rate dockets (Case Nos. 22-00286-UT and 20-

00238-UT) proved that SPS consistently incurs only 74.0% of its estimated rate case expenses,

evidencing padding.36

VI. RESPONSE REGARDING STAFF’S ALTERNATIVE TO TOTAL REJECTION OF
THE STIPULATION37
        Staff’s Exceptions proposed an alternative to total rejection of the $90.0 million stipulated

increase, proposing that the Commission condition approval on SPS submitting updated 2026 V-

1 financial load forecasts, current SPP resource-adequacy positions, recorded linkage data (July 1,

with rates made subject to refund.38 On November 4, 2026, SPS’s Motion asserted that Staff’s

alternative proposal was a “new remedy” that imposed severe administrative burdens.39 N

         NMSA 1978, Section 62-8-7(D), the Commission’s procedural rule for interim

rates,1.2.2.27 NMAC, and Supreme Court precedent, grant the Commission broad authority to

order a utility to make approved rates temporary and subject to refund pending final verification.40

Requiring SPS to submit verified, updated numbers prior to implementing an un-vetted $90 million

rate increase is an authorized to protect the public interest.

         Staff acknowledges that Section 2.7(b) of the Comprehensive Stipulation permits

Signatories to withdraw if the Commission modifies material terms. Staff also acknowledges that

under 1.2.2.20(B)(5) NMAC, the Commission possesses authority to adopt, reject, or modify any

proposed settlement. If the Commission adopts the Certification’s modifications, LES and FEA

may exercise their contractual right to withdraw and proceed to a hearing on the merits under

1.2.2.20(B) NMAC. However, their private contractual rights does not restrict the Commission’s

statutory duty to ensure that the end result of a rate case is to establish fair, just and reasonable

rates.

VIII. CONCLUSION WHEREFORE, Staff respectfully requests an Order:

(1) DENYING Exceptions filed by SPS, NMLCG and LES/FEA;(2) AFFIRMING AND
ADOPTING the Hearing Examiners’ recommended modifications set forth in Finding Paragraph
9 of the Certification of Stipulation, (3) GRANTING Staff’s Exceptions Nos. 1 through 9;(4)
GRANTING Staff’s Motion for Oral Argument
